I can't even seem to get a word out of my mouth about how terrible most post-Morrowind Bethesda RPG's are without being called "nostalgic", "entitled", or "whiny". All three of which are ridiculous for a number of reasons. I'll tell you this: My first Elder Scrolls game was Oblivion, and my first Fallout game was Fallout 3. I think both of them are pretty bad, and it wasn't really a matter of playing them and going, "wow, this sucks," it was a matter of playing other games in the series and going, "wow, this is what Fallout 3/Oblivion could have been."

Ever since Oblivion, Bethesda's main philosophy has been, "Let the player go anywhere anytime he wants, give him 100% freedom" Which sounds really amazing in theory, and this was even present in Morrowind. However, Morrowind offered the kind of freedom that should be present in an RPG, and not the "static sandbox" freedom present in Fallout 3, Oblivion, and Skyrim. In all 3 games, you never really feel like you're playing a game, it always just feels like a tourist ride and that everything is just laid out for you. The lore is shallow, the writing is pretty bad, and there are just no consequences for anything. All 3 points are what you got in order to get this "freedom" that does not reflect what the series (or even the genre) is supposed to stand for. Yeah, you can do any quest you want at any given time, how is that a good thing? Why should I be allowed to walk into any dungeon I want knowing everything is going to be scaled to my level?

But I'm not here to talk about the dumbing down of The Elder Scrolls, that topic has been done to death for the past 9 years, and I'm sure TES VI is going to piss off all fans of Morrowind. No, now that we've gotten 3 examples of Bethesda's mediocrity at the table, I'm here to talk about that atrocity that was the Fallout 4 E3 presentation.

Let me get one thing straight before I go any further. No, I don't think Fallout was ever about "Isometric Turn-Based RPG's". In fact, Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas is my favorite game of all time simply because of the immersion/roleplayablity it offers along with the lore, writing, dialogue, story, and just the sheer depth and detail of it.

The map design was actually relevant to the story/lore. You never saw a town without some kind of powerplant or farm nearby. The roads in the game actually served more than just "a way to get around without getting attacked by monsters" like in Bethesda games. In fact, the main quest actually had you loop around the map along the roads because the characters actually acknowledge the world around them instead of just being generic assholes with no backstory.

Every "dungeon"(interior areas, etc.) actually had their own story and actually had a reason to exist other than just for loot. None/very few of the monsters were scaled to my level because they don't give a shit how long I've been playing the game. This is what a Fallout game is to me. It's about exploring the world and the ethics of a post-apocalyptic America. "Do we really need some of these old world values?" "Let's not be so black and white here. Your decision might sound good in theory, but will have long term negative impact"

And Bethesda is destroying everything that Fallout stands for. Fallout 3 & 4 aren't really about the post-apocalyptic world. They're about the apocalypse, they just rub all of this "WOW ATOMIC NUKE" lore into your face. Look at the Fallout 4 E3 demo. There's a part where they play some song called "Atom Bomb Baby", why? In New Vegas, a lot of the songs were really reflective on the atmosphere and story of the game. Big Iron was reflective of the Courier as the Ranger, and Benny/Mr. House being Texas Red. Ain't That a Kick in the Head is about the starting events of the game, this is so obvious that the first quest you finish is called, "Ain't That a Kick in the Head". "Lone Star" is obviously about the Lucky 38 being seen out in the distance, and the rest of the songs are just really fitting with the atmosphere. Yet, Bethesda showcases their game with a song about an atomic bomb.

That's all Fallout is to them, just a generic post-apocalyptic setting with the goody two-shoes Brotherhood of Steel (my money's on their HQ being placed right in the middle of Boston) coming to save the day. Their RTS ""settlement building" mechanic has no business in a game that's supposed to be about roleplaying. Like I've said before, it sounds nice in theory, but it would be like filling Grand Theft Auto with Zelda-like puzzles. Both do well in their own games, we don't need these super cool jetpacks and laser explosions everywhere in Fallout.

And the voiced protagonist, oh god, I was going to get here eventually, but I didn't want to. A voiced protagonist with a dialogue wheel destroys all opportunity for role-playing and depth. Remember, these are the same people who gave Fallout 3 only two black and white endings and can apparently only afford 1 voice actor per 10 unique characters. (Like how Jarl Balgruuf of Riverwood tells you to warn Jarl Balgruuf of Whiterun about the Dragons) But don't worry, guys! Bethesda's a competent company that can't even program ladders. I'm sure this voiced protagonist with a 4-option dialogue wheel will have completely fleshed out lines with a deep and branching storyline. And if you don't want your character to sound like Troy Baker? Then you're simply entitled for wanting to play as a psychotic/nerdy/cowboy type character that you've played as in games with a silent protagonist.

Look, my point is Bethesda consistently makes these errors in the past, and from what we've seen we have every reason to believe that Bethesda is probably going to make them again with Fallout 4. I keep hearing people say, "wait until it's out! wait until it's out!", but these are the same people who are mindlessly hyped for a game so much that they can't even handle skepticism from others when it looks like Bethesda's butt cheeks are pointing right at our plates. Would you go to a restaurant that continuously serves shit and then order their chocolate pudding just because it has sprinkles this time? Why the hell would you do that?

I've been refraining from using this word the entire time, but I think the gaming market has been geared towards casuals for such a long time that we don't even know what that means anymore. Five years ago, you could go anywhere on the internet and ask what a casual gamer was. Easy enough, they'd tell you it's somebody who plays games that are too easy and too hand-holdy. Jump back here to 2015, now it just means hand-holdy, but in an entirely different sense. We've gone from "Call of Duty" to "mobile games" when it comes to the definition of casual. We've been knee-deep in shit for so long we've forgotten how it smells. Had Fallout 4 come out in 2010 instead of New Vegas, the controversy would be exponentially larger than it is now because the state of the market was apparently still good enough to warrant games like New Vegas, FEAR 2, and Portal 2.

I think game development companies are being too black and white about the information they gather from their sales. The gaming community has only gotten bigger since 2006, and for some reason they won't even bother to check if this was due to "streamlining" their games, or because of the impact the PS2 era had on games drawing more people in. I think most "casual" gamers could easily beat a relatively anti-casual game with minimal effort. It's always been in the nature of gamers to try shit out when we're given the ability to do so, hence why most modern Bethesda games are popular. It's just that it's been too long since we've seen an anti-casual AAA game with the same marketing as all these casual games. Look at New Vegas, that was a great game. It got a little casual at some points, but still left you on your own at a few spots. Yet it went under everyone's radar because it was released under the following conditions:

  • People were still playing Fallout 3
  • Skyrim had just been announced after 5 years of silence
  • The words "FALLOUT NEW VEGAS" weren't plastered all over our drinking cups and gaming sites

Game development companies have never tried to put marketting into non-casual games because they're thinking too black and white. They think of money as an information and then perform 1-step thinking to come to a conclusion that harms the entire industry. And I think we've grown to accustomed to that and we need to stop putting up with mediocrity. "Mods can fix it" should not be an excuse to buy a terrible game. We shouldn't have to put up with developers releasing games where putting a bucket over someone's head makes you practically invisible. We shouldn't be giving relentless praise to a game where you can nuke an entire town and make up for it by giving ONE GUY 2,000 caps, killing him, and getting your caps back. I know it sounds to some of you like the industry is moving forward, but what good is innovation without any kind of intuition?
